foundations.title: Professional Foundations — Ireland
foundations.action: Confirm your professional role, competence and any specialist authority needed.
foundations.record: Explain the purpose of involvement and how the person can influence assessment and planning. Separate the person’s wishes and evidence from organisational assumptions about risk or resources. Use the current CORU CPD guidance to turn supervision and feedback into demonstrable learning. A service complaint and a CORU fitness-to-practise concern address different issues. Help the person find the route relevant to the outcome they want, including the responsible organisation’s complaints and review processes.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — Ireland
care-support.action: Identify daily-living needs and which HSE service or other body is responsible for the requested support.
care-support.record: Use the relevant application and needs-assessment process, including discharge coordination if the person is in hospital. Separate the allocation of support from service availability, start dates and any other scheme’s financial assessment. Include family willingness, respite needs and a contingency if provision is delayed. Ask the responsible service for the assessment outcome, reasons and review or complaint route. HSE’s Home Support guidance explains applications and local contacts. Where more than one scheme is involved, track each decision and its challenge route separately.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Ireland
mca.action: State the precise decision and provide accessible information and communication support.
mca.record: Use the DSS capacity-assessment Code and record evidence against the relevant functional abilities. Read the actual agreement, registration or court order and verify what the supporter or representative can do. Check whether an applicable advance healthcare directive or other arrangement governs the healthcare decision. Use the appropriate DSS complaint or court route for concerns about arrangements or representatives. A disagreement about treatment may require clinical and legal advice under the HSE Consent Policy. Distinguish support to decide from authority to decide for someone.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Ireland
dols.action: Describe what happens if the person asks to leave and record their will and preferences.
dols.record: Check capacity for the relevant decision without treating incapacity as a detention authorisation. Use the current HSE Consent Policy and seek urgent legal advice where the person is held contrary to their wishes. Identify the precise court or mental-health authority relied on, its limits and a plan to reduce restrictions. Arrange independent support and access to legal advice where liberty is disputed. Court involvement and review must address the actual arrangement; a family meeting cannot confer the necessary power. Immediate action should not become indefinite confinement without review.

mha.title: Mental Health — Ireland
mha.action: Check the commencement record and current MHC operational guidance before choosing forms, criteria or time limits.
mha.record: Identify voluntary alternatives and the purpose of the proposed assessment, admission or treatment. Verify the authorised professionals and evidence required by the operative route. Arrange the applicable legal representation, independent review and treatment safeguards, and record which legal version was used. The person needs an accessible explanation of their status, legal support and the applicable tribunal or court process. A mental-health admission does not resolve every physical-health consent or accommodation decision. Check each intervention separately.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — Ireland
safeguarding.action: Identify the concern and safe contact arrangements, including coercion and dependency.
safeguarding.record: Use the service’s current safeguarding procedure and responsible HSE safeguarding route. Refer criminal or urgent safety issues to the appropriate Garda or emergency response where needed. Check consent, decision support and any legal authority separately from the protection plan. Ask about the adult’s desired outcomes and offer independent advocacy where appropriate. Explain the relevant service complaint, regulatory or DSS route. Record the policy version and whether a new national framework has been implemented through the service’s operative procedure.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Ireland
children.action: Establish whether you are a mandated person and whether the concern meets the statutory reporting threshold.
children.record: Report to Tusla through the correct process; follow emergency arrangements where a child is in immediate danger. Record the child’s words, the facts supporting the concern and what was reported. Coordinate family support, education and health, keeping any court or protection authority distinct. Explain the assessment or protection process and how the child and family can participate and obtain support or legal advice. A concern below the mandated threshold can still warrant a welfare report; the threshold is not a reason to ignore other needs.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Ireland
rights.action: Identify the right or equality duty engaged by the actual service decision.
rights.record: Consider accessibility, discrimination and the person’s preferred cultural and communication support. Document the legal basis and necessary scope of a disclosure, including consent or another applicable basis. Explain access, correction and the relevant service, equality or data-protection complaint route. IHREC provides public-sector duty guidance; the Data Protection Commission addresses data-protection matters. A service complaint or legal challenge may be needed for the underlying decision. Help the person identify the remedy and obtain advice within the applicable time limits.

sources.title: Ireland Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: CORU’s Social Workers Registration Board Code of Professional Conduct and Ethics is the professional anchor. Use the social-worker Code, rather than assuming that material for another CORU profession sets identical obligations. Registration, competence, confidentiality, professional boundaries and continuing learning need to be considered alongside the statutory function being performed.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: HSE services, Tusla, local authorities and voluntary providers have different remits. Establish whether the task concerns adult health and support, child protection, housing or another service, and identify who holds the decision-making responsibility.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Confirm your professional role, competence and any specialist authority needed. Explain the purpose of involvement and how the person can influence assessment and planning. Separate the person’s wishes and evidence from organisational assumptions about risk or resources. Use the current CORU CPD guidance to turn supervision and feedback into demonstrable learning.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: A service complaint and a CORU fitness-to-practise concern address different issues. Help the person find the route relevant to the outcome they want, including the responsible organisation’s complaints and review processes.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using another profession’s Code or assuming that an employer policy creates a statutory power.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: Map the actual HSE, disability, housing, income-support or nursing-home scheme. HSE Home Support for older people provides assistance with everyday tasks following assessment; it is generally directed to people aged 65 or over, with some younger people also eligible. The published service is free, but an assessment and funding decision must still be followed through to delivery.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Home Support, disability services and the Nursing Homes Support Scheme are distinct routes. Do not describe one approval as covering all care settings or assume that the rules for nursing-home financial support apply to home support.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify daily-living needs and which HSE service or other body is responsible for the requested support. Use the relevant application and needs-assessment process, including discharge coordination if the person is in hospital. Separate the allocation of support from service availability, start dates and any other scheme’s financial assessment. Include family willingness, respite needs and a contingency if provision is delayed.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Ask the responsible service for the assessment outcome, reasons and review or complaint route. HSE’s Home Support guidance explains applications and local contacts. Where more than one scheme is involved, track each decision and its challenge route separately.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating allocation of funding as evidence that a service has started, or conflating home-support and nursing-home schemes.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, as amended, uses a functional, decision- and time-specific approach. Presume capacity, provide support and consider understanding, retention, use or weighing of relevant information, and communication. The person’s will and preferences are central to the statutory approach.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Decision-making assistants, co-decision-makers and court-appointed decision-making representatives have different functions. Enduring powers of attorney and advance healthcare directives require their own checks. The Decision Support Service (DSS) registers or supervises relevant arrangements and provides Codes; it does not itself become the person’s decision-maker.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: State the precise decision and provide accessible information and communication support. Use the DSS capacity-assessment Code and record evidence against the relevant functional abilities. Read the actual agreement, registration or court order and verify what the supporter or representative can do. Check whether an applicable advance healthcare directive or other arrangement governs the healthcare decision.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Use the appropriate DSS complaint or court route for concerns about arrangements or representatives. A disagreement about treatment may require clinical and legal advice under the HSE Consent Policy. Distinguish support to decide from authority to decide for someone.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating every DSS arrangement as substitute decision-making or replacing will and preferences with professional convenience.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: Constitutional liberty and the applicable consent and mental-health law must be considered where a person is prevented from leaving a care setting. Incapacity, good intentions and relatives’ agreement do not supply general authority to detain.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The HSE National Consent Policy addresses deprivation of liberty and the need for legal advice and appropriate court involvement. Distinguish an ordinary care arrangement from detention, and distinguish a decision-support arrangement from authority for confinement. Do not start a new wardship process as though it remained the ordinary route after the decision-support reforms.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Describe what happens if the person asks to leave and record their will and preferences. Check capacity for the relevant decision without treating incapacity as a detention authorisation. Use the current HSE Consent Policy and seek urgent legal advice where the person is held contrary to their wishes. Identify the precise court or mental-health authority relied on, its limits and a plan to reduce restrictions.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Arrange independent support and access to legal advice where liberty is disputed. Court involvement and review must address the actual arrangement; a family meeting cannot confer the necessary power. Immediate action should not become indefinite confinement without review.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using consent to admission, a diagnosis or a relative’s signature as blanket authority to prevent departure.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Mental Health Act 2026 was signed into law on 7 May 2026. Section 1 provides for commencement by ministerial order, potentially on different dates for different provisions. Enactment must not be treated as evidence that all new admission, treatment or review rules have replaced the 2001 framework.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: For a real case, identify the operative provisions and current Mental Health Commission (MHC) guidance. The existing 2001 framework has separate application, medical recommendation and consultant-psychiatrist admission stages, with independent tribunal safeguards. Explain the route actually in force for the person rather than mixing stages from old and new legislation.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Check the commencement record and current MHC operational guidance before choosing forms, criteria or time limits. Identify voluntary alternatives and the purpose of the proposed assessment, admission or treatment. Verify the authorised professionals and evidence required by the operative route. Arrange the applicable legal representation, independent review and treatment safeguards, and record which legal version was used.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The person needs an accessible explanation of their status, legal support and the applicable tribunal or court process. A mental-health admission does not resolve every physical-health consent or accommodation decision. Check each intervention separately.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming that Royal Assent or publication means that every replacement procedure is already operational.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Department of Health published the National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care Sector in December 2025, with the publication page updated in February 2026. Read it alongside the operative HSE safeguarding procedures and the arrangements in the actual service. An older policy link alone does not describe the whole current policy picture.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Separate a safeguarding concern, a criminal matter, a provider-quality issue and a decision-support problem. HSE safeguarding services, An Garda Síochána, HIQA and the DSS have different remits. A safeguarding referral does not automatically create authority to override the adult’s decision.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the concern and safe contact arrangements, including coercion and dependency. Use the service’s current safeguarding procedure and responsible HSE safeguarding route. Refer criminal or urgent safety issues to the appropriate Garda or emergency response where needed. Check consent, decision support and any legal authority separately from the protection plan.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Ask about the adult’s desired outcomes and offer independent advocacy where appropriate. Explain the relevant service complaint, regulatory or DSS route. Record the policy version and whether a new national framework has been implemented through the service’s operative procedure.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating a national policy as a universal coercive power or overlooking service continuity after a report.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Children First Act 2015 creates reporting obligations for mandated persons; the Child Care Act 1991 supplies important child-welfare and protection functions. Tusla’s Children First guidance distinguishes the statutory harm threshold from other reasonable welfare concerns that should still be reported through the appropriate route.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: For mandated reporting, harm includes assault, ill-treatment or neglect seriously affecting or likely seriously to affect health, development or welfare, and sexual abuse. Apply the guidance for the category and circumstances, including its specific provisions on disclosures. Do not require proof before considering reasonable grounds.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Establish whether you are a mandated person and whether the concern meets the statutory reporting threshold. Report to Tusla through the correct process; follow emergency arrangements where a child is in immediate danger. Record the child’s words, the facts supporting the concern and what was reported. Coordinate family support, education and health, keeping any court or protection authority distinct.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the assessment or protection process and how the child and family can participate and obtain support or legal advice. A concern below the mandated threshold can still warrant a welfare report; the threshold is not a reason to ignore other needs.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Equating the mandated-report threshold with the only circumstances in which Tusla should receive a concern.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Equal Status Acts, constitutional rights, the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 and the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission Act 2014 form part of the rights map. The public-sector equality and human-rights duty requires public bodies to integrate equality and rights into their functions.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 govern personal-data processing alongside professional confidentiality and sector-specific duties. Identify the controller, purpose, lawful basis and any additional condition for sensitive data. A request from another agency does not itself establish permission to send a full record.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the right or equality duty engaged by the actual service decision. Consider accessibility, discrimination and the person’s preferred cultural and communication support. Document the legal basis and necessary scope of a disclosure, including consent or another applicable basis. Explain access, correction and the relevant service, equality or data-protection complaint route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: IHREC provides public-sector duty guidance; the Data Protection Commission addresses data-protection matters. A service complaint or legal challenge may be needed for the underlying decision. Help the person identify the remedy and obtain advice within the applicable time limits.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating public-sector status as unrestricted permission to share records.

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.
Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.
Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.
Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.
The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.
Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.
Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.
A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.
Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.
Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.
Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.
Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.
Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.
A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker is asked to describe a client as refusing support, although the only offer conflicts with the client’s religious practice and transport needs.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Record the actual offer and the reasons it was unsuitable. Explore an accessible alternative and bring any unresolved resource issue to supervision. A professional formulation should make the barrier visible rather than treating the organisation’s first offer as the only reasonable option.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An older person is ready to leave hospital, but the family is told that approved home-support funding means daily visits are already in place.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Confirm the provider, tasks, hours and first visit. Assess whether an interim plan is safe and agreed if staffing is unavailable. Keep the person’s preference for home, the family’s actual availability and any unmet need in the discharge record.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person has a decision-making assistance agreement and wants to refuse a proposed move. Staff ask the assistant to approve it instead.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Support the person to consider the actual options and record their wishes. Read the agreement: assistance is not replacement decision-making. If a separate assessment or court issue arises, identify it explicitly rather than expanding the assistant’s role.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A residential service says an adult cannot leave because the family signed the admission form. The adult repeatedly asks to go home.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Hear the adult with suitable support, establish the actual restrictions and examine the legal basis. Family agreement is not enough. Explore a workable alternative and obtain timely legal advice under the current consent policy about the necessary court or other lawful route.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A team circulates a summary of the newly enacted Act and proposes to use its future procedures for an admission immediately.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check whether the relevant provisions and forms have commenced. Use the operative law and current MHC instructions for the admission. Record the version check and keep preparation for reform separate from the person’s present legal safeguards.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An adult says a paid supporter controls their bank card but asks that the supporter not be dismissed because no replacement is available.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Explore coercion and immediate access to money, food and support. Make the appropriate safeguarding response while planning continuity of assistance. Consider whether a criminal, provider or decision-support concern also needs action; do not reduce the plan to removing one worker.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A child describes repeated lack of food and supervision. A worker is told to wait until the next team meeting to establish proof.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess immediate safety and the evidence of harm, use the relevant Tusla reporting threshold and act without waiting to prove the allegation. Record the child’s account accurately and arrange practical support alongside the protection response.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An agency requests a complete family file to decide whether to offer a transport service.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Clarify the purpose and the minimum information actually required, the lawful basis and any sensitive-data condition. Discuss participation and confidentiality with the person where appropriate. Record what is shared and why, rather than sending the file simply because the requester is another public body.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
CORU’s Social Workers Registration Board Code of Professional Conduct and Ethics is the professional anchor. Use the social-worker Code, rather than assuming that material for another CORU profession sets identical obligations. Registration, competence, confidentiality, professional boundaries and continuing learning need to be considered alongside the statutory function being performed.

HSE services, Tusla, local authorities and voluntary providers have different remits. Establish whether the task concerns adult health and support, child protection, housing or another service, and identify who holds the decision-making responsibility.

Local pathway:
Confirm your professional role, competence and any specialist authority needed.
Explain the purpose of involvement and how the person can influence assessment and planning.
Separate the person’s wishes and evidence from organisational assumptions about risk or resources.
Use the current CORU CPD guidance to turn supervision and feedback into demonstrable learning.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A service complaint and a CORU fitness-to-practise concern address different issues. Help the person find the route relevant to the outcome they want, including the responsible organisation’s complaints and review processes.

Sources:
https://coru.ie/about-us/legislation/registration-board-bye-laws/social-workers-registration-board-bye-laws/
https://www.coru.ie/health-and-social-care-professionals/continuing-professional-development/cpd-for-social-workers/

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Map the actual HSE, disability, housing, income-support or nursing-home scheme. HSE Home Support for older people provides assistance with everyday tasks following assessment; it is generally directed to people aged 65 or over, with some younger people also eligible. The published service is free, but an assessment and funding decision must still be followed through to delivery.

Home Support, disability services and the Nursing Homes Support Scheme are distinct routes. Do not describe one approval as covering all care settings or assume that the rules for nursing-home financial support apply to home support.

Local pathway:
Identify daily-living needs and which HSE service or other body is responsible for the requested support.
Use the relevant application and needs-assessment process, including discharge coordination if the person is in hospital.
Separate the allocation of support from service availability, start dates and any other scheme’s financial assessment.
Include family willingness, respite needs and a contingency if provision is delayed.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask the responsible service for the assessment outcome, reasons and review or complaint route. HSE’s Home Support guidance explains applications and local contacts. Where more than one scheme is involved, track each decision and its challenge route separately.

Sources:
https://www2.hse.ie/services/home-support-service/home-support-service-for-older-people/
https://www2.hse.ie/services/home-support-service/how-to-apply/

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, as amended, uses a functional, decision- and time-specific approach. Presume capacity, provide support and consider understanding, retention, use or weighing of relevant information, and communication. The person’s will and preferences are central to the statutory approach.

Decision-making assistants, co-decision-makers and court-appointed decision-making representatives have different functions. Enduring powers of attorney and advance healthcare directives require their own checks. The Decision Support Service (DSS) registers or supervises relevant arrangements and provides Codes; it does not itself become the person’s decision-maker.

Local pathway:
State the precise decision and provide accessible information and communication support.
Use the DSS capacity-assessment Code and record evidence against the relevant functional abilities.
Read the actual agreement, registration or court order and verify what the supporter or representative can do.
Check whether an applicable advance healthcare directive or other arrangement governs the healthcare decision.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Use the appropriate DSS complaint or court route for concerns about arrangements or representatives. A disagreement about treatment may require clinical and legal advice under the HSE Consent Policy. Distinguish support to decide from authority to decide for someone.

Sources:
https://www.decisionsupportservice.ie/resources/codes-practice/code-practice-supporting-decision-making-and-assessing-capacity
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2015/act/64/enacted/en/html
https://www.decisionsupportservice.ie/resources/guidance-materials

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Constitutional liberty and the applicable consent and mental-health law must be considered where a person is prevented from leaving a care setting. Incapacity, good intentions and relatives’ agreement do not supply general authority to detain.

The HSE National Consent Policy addresses deprivation of liberty and the need for legal advice and appropriate court involvement. Distinguish an ordinary care arrangement from detention, and distinguish a decision-support arrangement from authority for confinement. Do not start a new wardship process as though it remained the ordinary route after the decision-support reforms.

Local pathway:
Describe what happens if the person asks to leave and record their will and preferences.
Check capacity for the relevant decision without treating incapacity as a detention authorisation.
Use the current HSE Consent Policy and seek urgent legal advice where the person is held contrary to their wishes.
Identify the precise court or mental-health authority relied on, its limits and a plan to reduce restrictions.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Arrange independent support and access to legal advice where liberty is disputed. Court involvement and review must address the actual arrangement; a family meeting cannot confer the necessary power. Immediate action should not become indefinite confinement without review.

Sources:
https://www2.healthservice.hse.ie/organisation/national-pppgs/hse-national-consent-policy/

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health Act 2026 was signed into law on 7 May 2026. Section 1 provides for commencement by ministerial order, potentially on different dates for different provisions. Enactment must not be treated as evidence that all new admission, treatment or review rules have replaced the 2001 framework.

For a real case, identify the operative provisions and current Mental Health Commission (MHC) guidance. The existing 2001 framework has separate application, medical recommendation and consultant-psychiatrist admission stages, with independent tribunal safeguards. Explain the route actually in force for the person rather than mixing stages from old and new legislation.

Local pathway:
Check the commencement record and current MHC operational guidance before choosing forms, criteria or time limits.
Identify voluntary alternatives and the purpose of the proposed assessment, admission or treatment.
Verify the authorised professionals and evidence required by the operative route.
Arrange the applicable legal representation, independent review and treatment safeguards, and record which legal version was used.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The person needs an accessible explanation of their status, legal support and the applicable tribunal or court process. A mental-health admission does not resolve every physical-health consent or accommodation decision. Check each intervention separately.

Sources:
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/act/11/section/1/enacted/en/html
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/press-releases/mental-health-act-2026-signed-into-law-by-president-connolly/
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2001/act/25/enacted/en/html
https://www.mhcirl.ie/

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Department of Health published the National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care Sector in December 2025, with the publication page updated in February 2026. Read it alongside the operative HSE safeguarding procedures and the arrangements in the actual service. An older policy link alone does not describe the whole current policy picture.

Separate a safeguarding concern, a criminal matter, a provider-quality issue and a decision-support problem. HSE safeguarding services, An Garda Síochána, HIQA and the DSS have different remits. A safeguarding referral does not automatically create authority to override the adult’s decision.

Local pathway:
Identify the concern and safe contact arrangements, including coercion and dependency.
Use the service’s current safeguarding procedure and responsible HSE safeguarding route.
Refer criminal or urgent safety issues to the appropriate Garda or emergency response where needed.
Check consent, decision support and any legal authority separately from the protection plan.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask about the adult’s desired outcomes and offer independent advocacy where appropriate. Explain the relevant service complaint, regulatory or DSS route. Record the policy version and whether a new national framework has been implemented through the service’s operative procedure.

Sources:
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/publications/national-policy-framework-for-adult-safeguarding-in-the-health-and-social-care-sector/
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/publications/adult-safeguarding/

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Children First Act 2015 creates reporting obligations for mandated persons; the Child Care Act 1991 supplies important child-welfare and protection functions. Tusla’s Children First guidance distinguishes the statutory harm threshold from other reasonable welfare concerns that should still be reported through the appropriate route.

For mandated reporting, harm includes assault, ill-treatment or neglect seriously affecting or likely seriously to affect health, development or welfare, and sexual abuse. Apply the guidance for the category and circumstances, including its specific provisions on disclosures. Do not require proof before considering reasonable grounds.

Local pathway:
Establish whether you are a mandated person and whether the concern meets the statutory reporting threshold.
Report to Tusla through the correct process; follow emergency arrangements where a child is in immediate danger.
Record the child’s words, the facts supporting the concern and what was reported.
Coordinate family support, education and health, keeping any court or protection authority distinct.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the assessment or protection process and how the child and family can participate and obtain support or legal advice. A concern below the mandated threshold can still warrant a welfare report; the threshold is not a reason to ignore other needs.

Sources:
https://www.tusla.ie/children-first/mandated-persons/what-are-the-thresholds-for-making-a-mandated-report/
https://www.tusla.ie/children-first/children-first-guidance-and-legislation/
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2015/act/36/enacted/en/html

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Equal Status Acts, constitutional rights, the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 and the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission Act 2014 form part of the rights map. The public-sector equality and human-rights duty requires public bodies to integrate equality and rights into their functions.

GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 govern personal-data processing alongside professional confidentiality and sector-specific duties. Identify the controller, purpose, lawful basis and any additional condition for sensitive data. A request from another agency does not itself establish permission to send a full record.

Local pathway:
Identify the right or equality duty engaged by the actual service decision.
Consider accessibility, discrimination and the person’s preferred cultural and communication support.
Document the legal basis and necessary scope of a disclosure, including consent or another applicable basis.
Explain access, correction and the relevant service, equality or data-protection complaint route.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
IHREC provides public-sector duty guidance; the Data Protection Commission addresses data-protection matters. A service complaint or legal challenge may be needed for the underlying decision. Help the person identify the remedy and obtain advice within the applicable time limits.

Sources:
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2014/act/25/section/42/enacted/en/html
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2018/act/7/enacted/en/html
https://www.coru.ie/files-codes-of-conduct/swrb-code-of-professional-conduct-and-ethics-for-social-workers.pdf
